River redhorse (Moxostoma carinatum) reaches a considerable ultimate total length of 77 cm [Li = 77 cm], a size that distinguishes it among the larger-bodied members of the genus Moxostoma. Field surveys conducted across the Mississippi River basin indicate that this species attains such dimensions only after an extended period of growth, typically spanning a decade or more under favorable conditions. The species is also characterized by a total length at puberty of 34 cm [Lp = 34 cm], a threshold that marks the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the individual's transition from the sub-adult phase to reproductive viability. This length-based metric for pubertal onset is commonly used in catostomid studies, as it provides a direct, non-lethal proxy for maturity in the field. The substantial gap between the length at which reproduction begins and the maximum recorded size suggests a long reproductive window, during which fecundity and egg quality may increase with further somatic expansion.

Despite its large ultimate size, the life history of River redhorse begins at a remarkably small scale. The wet weight at birth, reflecting the mass of the newly hatched yolk-sac larva, is approximately 0.0056 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0056 grams], a value derived from the diameter of the demersal, adhesive eggs typical of this lineage. This minute initial mass underscores the highly endotrophic, lecithotrophic phase that follows egg fertilisation and hatching; the yolk-sac larva subsists entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves during the first days post-eclosion. The low energetic demands of this yolk-dependent embryo allow the species to invest in comparatively large clutches without an excessive maternal burden. Observations of related catostomids suggest that the onset of exogenous feeding typically occurs within the first week after hatching, at which point the prolarva transitions to an actively foraging, exotrophic larva.

This annual reproductive investment is considerable, reflecting the high fecundity typical of iteroparous catostomids that broadcast spawn over gravel substrates. The temperature during the spawning period is a critical environmental cue, as it synchronises gamete release and subsequent embryonation. The daily fecundity estimate, when scaled across the entire breeding season, indicates that a single gravid female may deposit tens of thousands of eggs annually, though survival to the juvenile stage remains low due to predation on the planktonic larvae.

Adults of River redhorse achieve a wet weight at puberty of approximately 329.5 grams [Wwp = approximately 329.5 grams], a body mass that correlates closely with the 34 cm length threshold for gonadal activation. This mass is attained after several years of growth, during which the juvenile transitions through the fingerling and sub-adult stages. The wet weight at puberty represents a critical energetic benchmark; individuals below this mass rarely exhibit the gonadal recrudescence necessary for successful spawning. In comparative terms, this value is somewhat higher than that reported for smaller-bodied catostomid species such as the white sucker (Catostomus commersonii), reflecting the River redhorse's more extended juvenile period and its preference for larger, deeper river channels where food resources are patchier. The ultimate wet weight for this species is an estimated 3670 grams [Wwi = 3670 grams], a figure that highlights the substantial somatic investment required to sustain a fish capable of living for many years.

Longevity data for River redhorse indicate a maximum lifespan of 15 years [am = 15 years] when individuals are maintained at an average annual water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This extended lifespan, quite typical of large-bodied, iteroparous catostomids in temperate rivers, allows multiple reproductive bouts across a long adult phase. The old age of such individuals is often inferred from scale annuli or otolith thin sections, which reveal a slow but steady growth trajectory that plateaus only at the largest size classes. Senescence in this species is gradual; even after reproductive senescence begins, older individuals may still spawn intermittently. The thermal regime of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] is characteristic of the species' core distribution in the upper Mississippi and Ohio River drainages, where summer temperatures rarely exceed this threshold. This relatively cool environment likely contributes to the extended lifespan by reducing metabolic costs and oxidative damage over the long term.
